Our first radio programme

When our English club decided to make a short radio programme, I was excited but nervous. None of us had spoken into a studio（录音室） microphone（麦克风） before. We wanted to produce something that students would actually enjoy, rather than another list of school announcements（公告）.

According to our list of agreed duties（职责）, I was for organising（组织） the interviews（采访）. Before choosing our guests（嘉宾）, we a short survey（调查） to find out what our listeners（听众） wanted. Many asked to hear about unusual（不寻常的） hobbies, so we invited（邀请） a student who repairs（修理） old bicycles（自行车）.

he was confident（自信的） when talking to us in the playground, he became quiet in the studio（录音室）. We moved the microphone（麦克风） to a smaller room and chatted for a few minutes before recording（录音）. This helped him feel at ease. The recording（录音） was borrowed（借来的） from a local media centre, and a volunteer showed us how to operate（操作） its controls（控制装置）.

We divided（分成） the programme three sections: an interview, a book recommendation（推荐） and a short quiz. During editing（剪辑）, we could hear every voice, but some words ran together. Those lines needed to be spoken more . We recorded them again to confusing（令人困惑的） our listeners（听众）.

Our teacher introduced us to a former（以前的） pupil job involves producing（制作） podcasts（播客）. Until then, we had doubted our ability（能力） to manage the final edit. Her practical（实用的） advice gave us the to finish the programme ourselves. It took longer than we expected, but the effort was it when classmates asked when the next episode（集） would be available.

Reading Part 3

Article · Paragraphs 1–4

A different way to see our town

A different way to see our town

Read the article first. 先阅读文章，再讨论题目。

1When my aunt asked me to help create a walking map of our town, I nearly said no. I had lived there all my life and thought there was little worth（值得的） showing visitors（访客）. The shopping centre was easy to find, and the famous waterfall（瀑布） was outside town. Besides, I imagined spending my school holiday measuring roads. My aunt, who runs a small guesthouse（民宿）, suggested that I join just one walk before deciding. I agreed, mainly because I did not want to disappoint（令……失望） her.

2Our first stop was a narrow lane behind the market. I had passed its entrance hundreds of times without going in. My aunt introduced me to Mr Lim, who repaired umbrellas in a workshop（工作坊） no larger than our kitchen. While replacing a broken handle, he explained how the market had changed since his childhood（童年）. I had expected to collect names and opening times. Instead, I found myself asking questions about people. For the first time, an ordinary（普通的） lane seemed to have a story.

3I planned the first route（路线） on my laptop. The software connected twelve interesting places in the shortest possible distance, which looked impressive on the screen. My aunt was less convinced. She asked where visitors（访客） would pause, whether they could cross the busy road easily and how much shade（阴凉处） they would find at midday. I had treated a walk as a race between points. A useful route（路线）, I began to realise, had to consider the experience between the stops as well as the stops themselves. The shortest route（路线） also passed a noisy loading（装卸货） area. A slightly longer path beside the river offered somewhere to sit, and we chose that option instead.

4To test it, we invited（邀请） two neighbours（邻居） who did not know the area well. I expected them to finish in forty minutes. They took almost twice as long, stopping to read signs and ask questions. One missed a turning（转弯处） because my instruction said, "Turn after the blue shop." There were two blue shops. Rather than blame our testers for being slow, I rewrote the directions using street names and clear landmarks（地标）. We also removed two stops so that people would have time to look around.

Reading Part 3

Article · Paragraphs 5–7

A different way to see our town

A different way to see our town

Read the article first. 先阅读文章，再讨论题目。

5Another question（质疑） was how to describe the route（路线） for visitors（访客） with different needs. At first, I wanted to put a single "easy access" symbol beside the whole walk. Then one neighbour pointed out a step at a cafe entrance and a rough stretch of pavement（人行道）. A broad label would hide details that could matter to someone. We measured the narrowest（最狭窄的） paths and recorded where steps occurred. Our map now gives those facts, allowing visitors（访客） to decide which sections suit them. We also explain that conditions may change. Visitors（访客） can send us corrections, but we check each report in person before changing the map. A comment about a closed gate, for example, might describe a temporary（暂时的） problem rather than a permanent（永久的） barrier（障碍）.

6Not everyone welcomed the project immediately. A shopkeeper worried that groups would block his doorway（门口）, while a resident did not want her home included in photographs（照片）. We listened and suggested visiting the shop at a quieter time. The resident's house was left off the map. These conversations（谈话） took longer than drawing lines on a screen, but they reminded me that an interesting place is also somebody's everyday space. Inviting visitors（访客） should not mean ignoring the people who already live there.

7The finished map is available both on paper and on a simple webpage. We chose not to build an expensive app: visitors（访客） should not need to download anything for a short walk. Each month, a volunteer checks the route（路线） and updates any changed details. I still use digital tools, but I no longer assume that a neat line on a screen tells the whole story. Now, when friends say there is nothing to do in our town, I invite them to take a walk with me.

Reading Part 4

Questions 27–32

Gapped text · A–H with two extra sentences

Making room for a garden

Six sentences are missing. Tap gaps 27–32 and select from A–H. Each sentence can be used once. 两项多余选项。

Our youth centre's garden began with a promise: the paved（铺了地砖的） yard would remain available for events. Our drawing placed wheeled containers（容器） in the centre for gardening（园艺） and along the walls during events. The manager asked how we would get them from one arrangement（安排） to the other. To find out before ordering（订购）, we borrowed（借来的） two full containers（容器） and tried moving them while another group set out chairs.

The trial（试行） changed more than the positions on our drawing. A container could pass between two rows of chairs, but the person pushing it had nowhere to stand when turning（转弯处）. We altered（修改了） the layout（布局） together, instead of asking either group to work around the other's finished arrangement（安排）.

Growing the plants brought a less visible problem. Although everyone signed the list after a visit, some pots received water twice and others not at all. Adding more names would not solve that. We changed the list so volunteers（志愿者） recorded the condition of each pot and what they had done, leaving the next person something useful to act on.

When the first tomatoes appeared, someone suggested dividing them according to the number of visits recorded. It sounded fair（公平的） until we remembered members who had repaired containers（容器） or found donated（捐赠的） tools. We dropped the counting idea and invited（邀请） everyone who had helped to share the harvest（收成）.

A shared lunch seemed a good solution, but several helpers could not attend that day. We set aside（留出） portions（份量） for collection（收取） later rather than treating absence（缺席） from the meal as absence（缺席） from the project. The harvest（收成） was small, yet nobody's contribution had to disappear with it.

The garden's first film evening put our arrangements to the test. One helper was away, so an event volunteer joined the moving team. They checked the route（路线） together and adjusted（调整的） the chairs before touching a container. The useful lesson was not that our first plan had been perfect, but that people now knew how to adapt（调整） it together.

Questions 37–40

One-word answers from the source texts

Learning through experience

Complete each gap with NO MORE THAN ONE WORD from the six accounts. 每题只能填一个原文词。

These experiences show that learning involves more than following instructions. In photography（摄影）, noticing a worthwhile（值得的） subject depended on rather than the price of the camera. Elsewhere, practical（实用的） training made routine（日常的） bicycle maintenance（维修） easier to manage: one learner could now deal with a flat tyre（爆胎） and adjust the . Keeping evidence of a process served different purposes. A preserved（保存了） cooking details that had previously gone unmeasured, while regular made slow changes in growing plants easier to recognise（辨认）. In both cases, a record（记录） revealed something that memory or a quick glance might miss.
